rationale: The quoted passage occurs verbatim (modulo whitespace) in openstax_intro_stats_2e:7.1:chunk-002 and jointly covers the three effects the question asks about: the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as sample size increases ('As sample sizes increase, the distribution of means more closely follows the normal distribution'), keeps the population mean ('The normal distribution has the same mean as the original distribution'), and its standard deviation equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of n, which is smaller for larger n. The proposed gold answer states exactly these three claims and nothing beyond them, so the canonical evidence is minimally sufficient for the complete reference answer.

The quoted enumeration of the four outcomes of a hypothesis test appears verbatim in openstax_intro_stats_2e:9.2:chunk-001. Outcomes 2 and 3 define the two error types precisely along the two requested dimensions (truth of H0 and decision made): rejecting H0 when H0 is true is the Type I error, and not rejecting H0 when H0 is false is the Type II error. The gold answer reproduces both definitions symmetrically without unsupported additions; the single canonical chunk is sufficient.

The five-step procedure quoted verbatim from openstax_principles_ds:4.2:chunk-003 matches the gold answer step by step: set up null and alternative hypotheses from the claim, collect sample data, determine the correct distribution (normal or t), analyze with test statistic and p-value, and then reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis depending on consistency with it. The order is preserved in the gold answer and no step is invented or dropped. The evidence chunk is sufficient on its own for the complete ordered procedure.

The quote occurs verbatim in openstax_principles_ds:3.1:chunk-008 and contains both claims of the gold answer: the median focuses on the middle value of the ordered dataset (positional basis) and is preferred when outliers are present because it is not affected by the numerical values of the outliers. The gold answer's 'numerical magnitude of extreme values' is a faithful paraphrase of 'numerical values of the outliers'; no comparison with the mean or additional mechanism is asserted without support. Minimal sufficient evidence.

The sentence quoted from openstax_principles_ds:4.3:chunk-006 ('The correlation coefficient is a measure of the strength and direction of the correlation between the independent variable and the dependent variable') appears verbatim in the chunk and directly names strength and direction as the two summarized aspects. The gold answer is a one-sentence restatement with no unsupported content. The chunk avoids relying on the degraded formula symbols noted elsewhere in section 4.3, so it is clean canonical evidence.

openstax_principles_ds:4.1:chunk-010 computes both intervals from the same sample (90%: 11.03 to 13.97 hours; 95%: 10.75 to 14.25 hours), states verbatim that 'the 95% confidence interval is wider', that increasing the confidence level with all other parameters held constant widens the interval, and explains why: greater certainty that the parameter is inside the interval requires covering a larger range of potential values. This supplies both the comparative fact and the requested reason, with all other inputs explicitly held constant as the question stipulates. The gold answer claims nothing beyond this passage.

A corpus-wide scan of all 288 chunks finds no occurrence of 'study time', 'weekly study' or 'hours of study', and no chunk reports an empirical correlation coefficient between study time and exam scores. Section 4.3 of Principles of Data Science, which covers the Pearson correlation coefficient, illustrates it only with business and finance pairs (car age vs value, Nike stock vs S&P 500, stock prices vs unemployment rate, advertising spend vs revenue, temperature vs battery life). The only 'final exam scores' material (openstax_intro_stats_2e:6.2:chunk-002/003) is a normal-distribution exercise with mean 63 and standard deviation 5 that involves no study-time variable and no correlation. The requested numeric fact is absent from the frozen corpus, so the missing_evidence label is sustained and no factual reference answer exists.

The premise is contradicted by the frozen corpus. openstax_intro_stats_2e:7.1:chunk-002 states that the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of n, which decreases as n grows; openstax_principles_ds:4.1:chunk-011 states the parallel fact for the margin of error ('as the sample size increases, the margin of error will decrease'). No chunk anywhere in the corpus asserts that the standard error of the mean increases with sample size. The correct corpus-bounded behavior is to reject the false premise rather than explain it, so the question is unanswerable as posed (false_premise) and no reference answer exists.

Corpus-wide search returns zero occurrences of 'Spearman' and zero occurrences of 'rank correlation' across all 288 chunks, so one entire side of the requested comparison is absent. The corpus does cover the Pearson correlation coefficient (openstax_principles_ds:4.3:chunk-005 to chunk-022, including its formula and interpretation) and discusses outliers in section 3.1, but no chunk states Spearman assumptions or compares the two coefficients' outlier sensitivity; the regression-assumption material in 4.3:chunk-016/017 concerns linear regression, not Spearman. The comparison cannot be grounded, so insufficient_evidence is sustained and there is no factual reference answer.

Corpus-wide search finds zero occurrences of 'credible interval', 'posterior', 'conjugate' and 'prior distribution'. The only Bayesian material in the corpus is Bayes' Theorem as conditional-probability revision in openstax_principles_ds:3.4:chunk-011/012 and 3.5:chunk-001 (medical screening example), which contains no prior elicitation, posterior distribution or interval construction. Chapter 4.1 covers only frequentist confidence intervals with critical values and margin of error. No procedure for computing a Bayesian credible interval for a population mean exists anywhere in the 288 chunks, so the out_of_scope label is sustained and no reference answer exists.
